scenes.note: What if you could read minds? Imagine for a moment.
You're sitting in a coffee shop, minding your own business.
And suddenly, you hear it. Not the clinking of cups.
Not the hiss of the espresso machine.
But the thoughts of everyone around you.
The barista: "I hate this job.

I hope that guy doesn't tip again."
The businessman: "My wife doesn't know about the account in Cayman Islands."
The teenager: "I'm pregnant.

Mom's gonna kill me."
The elderly couple: "Forty years and he still doesn't know I never liked his mother."

At first, it feels like a superpower.
The ultimate advantage. You'd know every lie before it's spoken.
Every secret before it's hidden. Every intention before it's acted upon.
Negotiations? You'd win every time. Relationships? You'd never be blindsided. Poker?
You'd clean the table. But then... the noise begins.

[pause]

Because here's the thing about human minds.
They're not clean, organized libraries. They're chaotic, messy, contradictory storms.
Every person carries: regret about yesterday. Anxiety about tomorrow.
Fantasies they'd never act on. Judgments they'd never voice.
Desires they'd never admit. Shame they carry like a second skin.

[pause]

And now... you hear ALL of it. Simultaneously. Without filters.

Without an off switch. [long pause]

The coffee shop becomes a cacophony.
Hundreds of inner voices screaming at once. The barista's resentment.
The businessman's guilt. The teenager's terror.
The elderly woman's decades of suppressed resentment. Your head pounds.
You can't focus. You can't think your OWN thoughts because everyone else's are drowning them out.

[pause]

You try to leave. But on the street, it's worse.

The driver in the passing car: "I should just drive off this bridge."
The mother with the stroller: "I don't think I love this baby enough."
The jogger: "Three miles.
Only three. I'm so fat. I'm so weak.

Why bother?"

[pause]

Every person you pass carries a universe of pain you never asked to witness.
Privacy isn't just a social construct. It's a survival mechanism.
The walls between minds exist for a reason.

[short pause]

Because thoughts are not actions.
A fleeting fantasy of violence doesn't make someone a killer.
A moment of doubt doesn't mean they don't love you.
A secret shame doesn't define their character. But when you KNOW...
when you HEAR it all... the context is lost.
The nuance is gone. You just have the raw, ugly data.

[pause]

Your partner thinks: "He's gained weight." — You hear: "He's disgusting."
Your friend thinks: "I'm jealous of her promotion." — You hear: "She doesn't deserve it."
Your boss thinks: "Maybe I'm not cut out for this." — You hear: "I'm a fraud."

[pause]

The intimacy that makes relationships beautiful — the mystery, the trust, the choice to be vulnerable — evaporates.
Because there's no CHOICE anymore. No slow reveal. No earned trust.

Just... exposure. [long pause]

And the worst part?

You can't unhear it. [pause]

That terrible thought your mother had about you when you were five?
You hear it now. At her funeral.
That cruel joke your best friend made in his head?
You hear it at his wedding.
That moment of doubt your child had about loving you?
You hear it on their birthday.

[long pause]

You learn to fake it.
To smile when you hear the ugly thoughts.
To pretend you don't know. To build walls inside your own mind to protect yourself from theirs.

[pause]

But sometimes... the walls crack.
And in those moments of weakness, you hear something you wish you could unhear.
A thought of betrayal that was never acted upon.
A moment of cruelty that was only imagined.
A secret that was never told.

[pause]

And you realize: the real curse isn't hearing thoughts.
The real curse is knowing how much ugliness lives in every human heart — including your own.

[long pause]

Because here's the truth: we're all terrible, sometimes.
We all have dark thoughts. Shameful desires. Cruel impulses.
The difference is... most of us don't act on them.
Most of us choose to be better than our worst moments.
But when you HEAR the worst moments of everyone...

you lose faith in that choice. [pause]

So you isolate.
You wear noise-canceling headphones that don't work. You avoid crowds.
You stop looking people in the eye.
You become a ghost in your own life.

[pause]

Until one day, you meet someone whose mind is... quiet.
Not empty. Not simple. Just... peaceful. Organized.
They think in complete sentences. They feel without chaos.
They exist without the constant storm.
And for the first time in years... you can breathe.

[pause]

You realize then: the superpower isn't reading minds.
The superpower is finding someone whose mind you WANT to read.
Someone whose chaos matches yours. Someone whose noise becomes music.

[pause]

And you learn: we don't need to read minds to connect.
We need to choose to listen. To ask. To be vulnerable.
To trust that the person across from us is more than their worst thought.

[long pause]

Because the walls between minds? They're not prisons.
They're gardens. And what grows there...
that's for each of us to tend. And to share.
Only when we're ready. Only with those who've earned it.

[soft pause]

Time to take off the headphones.
The coffee shop is just a coffee shop.
The barista's just tired. The businessman's just human.
The teenager's just scared. And you? You're just you.

Finally, blessedly, just you. [soft laugh]

The real mind-reading was the friends we made along the way.

[long pause]

The end.
